body:
Pick a short fable and read it together — then ask: what would YOU have done if you were the fox? The crow? The ant?
Kids reveal so much when the lesson belongs to a character, not to them.
Safer to be honest when it's not technically about you. 🦊

I didn't plan anything. I just said: figure out what you want to do today.
Watching them negotiate that — without me stepping in — taught me more than any structured activity ever did.

body:
Say a simple word out loud — 'cat,' 'sun,' 'dog' — and ask your kid to draw it before they spell it.
That tiny gap between hearing and drawing is where new words actually land.
Works in any language. Works especially well with English if it's not their first.

Bedtime used to be when I'd catch up — sneak in a little reading practice, make it feel casual.
But the nights she chose the book herself, chose when to stop, chose what to reread — something shifted.
She wasn't just reading. She was deciding. That part mattered more than I expected.

body:
Somewhere along the way I stopped finishing her sentences when she was deciding something.
Even when I could see the answer faster than she could.
Watching her find it herself took longer. It also stuck longer.
That pause I had to hold — that was the real work.

One of my daughters would only sit still for learning activities if her sister was doing them too — not competing, just present.
That companionship thing is real. Side by side changes the whole feeling of it.
That observation quietly shaped a lot of what went into the Little Detectives 5-in-1 Learning Bundle.

I used to tell my daughters the moral of every story before they had a chance to find it themselves.
It took me years to realize I was stealing the best part.
The moment they sit with a story and work out what it means — that's when it actually lands.

Something about the letters felt too far from play — too much like sitting still and being tested.
That disconnect is what I kept coming back to when I made My First ABC Adventure.

Everyone assumed she was fine. She wasn't. She was waiting for someone to notice she felt left out of a conversation she didn't have the words for yet.
Sometimes the loudest thing a kid can feel is the one nobody sees.

She used to ask me which book to pick at bedtime.
I'd choose fast — practical, tired, ready to be done.
The nights I made myself wait, she'd eventually reach for one herself. And she'd read longer.
That small pause cost me nothing. What she built from it was hers.
